newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN WHITE COLLAR CRIME TEAMS BOGGED DOWN.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN WHITE COLLAR CRIME TEAMS BOGGED DOWN.

text.p: Frustration with bureaucracy, tight budgets and staff shortages boiled over in the parliamentary public accounts committee on Wednesday.

In the dock were top justice officials who had to explain why the Department of Justice's Office for Serious Economic Offences (OSEO) had declared a moratorium on new cases of white collar crime being investigated because of staff shortages.
OSEO director-general Jan Swanepoel admitted that the problem of escalating white collar crime was serious but he did not have the staff, particularly advocates, to keep up with new cases.
It had therefore been decided to dispose of crimes already being investigated before further cases were taken on.
Although OSEO had managed to convince some organisations to help fund investigation teams for white collar crimes, it had not been able to get the go-ahead to fill 29 extra posts.
Swanepoel and Justice director-general Jasper Noeth described how they had been shunted from department to department in search of funds to take on extra staff.
He said Justice Minister Dullah Omar had also done what he could to persuade various authorities that extra staff were needed.

"But every time we have discussions, they refer you to somebody else. The decision should be taken now. Either the money is available to create these posts or the money is not available and if it is not available, it should be said."

But the committee was criticial of the fact that the department had turned in millions of rands in unspent funds each year, indicating that budgets were not being efficiently managed and that the funds were available.

It was told, however, that "the rules" stipulated that so-called rollover funds could not be used for recurrent expenditure. There was some confusion among officials and committee members whether funds allocated for accountants could be used to employ advocates.
At the same time, the committee heard that the filling of what empty posts were available had been delayed by wrangles over affirmative action appointments.
"We are embroiled in one of the worst quagmires of bureaucratic procedures that I have yet seen," African National Congress (ANC) MP Barbara Hogan said.

"If I was a person intent on doing serious economic crime, I would have no problem about going ahead with it because what we have here is a sorry case of everyone blaming everyone else and nothing really being done."
The last time OSEO had appeared before the committee in 1995, the same problems had been highlighted and there seemed to have been little progress.
"What we perhaps need is a total re-think," she said.

The 1995 recommendation by the committee that a task team be appointed to investigate how serious economic crime was dealt with should be implemented. This should include ways to improve the conditions of service of OSEO staff.
